cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents to receive credits from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive refunds after the city secured a $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro. Both the city and company filed lawsuits against each other in 2021 during the pandemic. The city alleged that Waste Pro failed to meet its contractual service standards, while the company attributed the problems to labor shortages caused by the pandemic. The city council voted unanimously to return all settlement funds to residents through credits applied to property tax bills instead of issuing physical checks.

The settlement amounts vary depending on residents' circumstances. More than 5,700 households that have maintained the same owner since 2022 will receive $364 credits, as these properties experienced the most severe service disruptions during the pandemic. Thousands of other homes will receive a $64 credit to account for rate increases that occurred while Waste Pro breached its contract. These rate increases covered expenses including a new waste site construction, litigation costs, and transitioning to a new waste provider. Councilman David Pickett emphasized that residents who endured the service failures deserve to be compensated for their suffering.

The city faces challenges in distributing funds to properties that changed ownership. The city identified 24,676 properties with title changes since 2022 and 13,241 newly constructed properties. Because the city cannot determine whether ownership changes resulted from trusts, marriage, divorce, or relocation, and cannot locate former owners, these properties will receive the $64 credit. Residents who sold a home and purchased another within the city during this period can submit documentation proving continuous ownership to claim the remaining $300 credit. A 180-day claims window will allow qualified residents to receive the additional credit on their following year's property tax bill, once the claims process is established and reviewed by city staff and the legal department.

Mayor Shannon Martin stated that the funds should benefit residents who experienced the service issues in 2021 and 2022. Resident Kelly Lee expressed satisfaction with the council's decision, saying she was "pleasantly surprised with the outcome" and that "the city presented well thought out plans." Councilman Anthony Bonna indicated the settlement struck an appropriate balance, noting the city had "reached the sweet spot here." The distribution of settlement funds through property tax credits provides direct relief to Port St. Lucie residents while acknowledging the varying degrees of impact the service failures had on different households.

cards.headline: Martin County residents push for public pool at high school, call for November referendum
cards.teaser: Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an.
cards.body:
Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an affordable resource for swim education. Patty Beonde, whose brother drowned at 30 years old, spoke at the meeting. She said her brother was caught in an undertow and had never had swimming lessons. Ricki Stein, a Martin County resident, said free access is key to getting children comfortable in the water. Dick Landrum, another Martin County resident, said affordability is central to the effort, noting that several venues in Martin County teach people how to swim but most are costly.

The nonprofit Martin Swims asked local leaders to put a referendum on the November ballot that would create a fund to establish community pools. They suggested residents pay less than $10 a year per property to fund the pool on the Martin County High School campus. Both county and school district leaders expressed support for the idea. Martin County Commissioner Ed Ciampi said he is in favor of letting the public decide on the importance of swimming education. Martin County School District Superintendent Michael Maine said he is already making plans to set up a meeting with Martin Swims to explore the logistics. Dr. Blanche Wells, president of Martin Swims, said the cause is personal and urgent and that those involved are devoted to it because it is life-saving.

cards.headline: Florida CFO claims Palm Beach County wasted $1.2 billion over six years
cards.teaser: Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia held a news conference in Boca Raton, claiming Palm Beach County tallied $1.23 billion since 2020 in excessive and wasteful spending.
cards.body:
Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia held a news conference Tuesday at Palm Beach State College in Boca Raton, claiming Palm Beach County has engaged in $1.23 billion in "excessive and wasteful spending" since 2020. Using his Florida Agency for Fiscal Oversight methodology, Ingoglia said this represents money collected beyond what the county needed to run local government, accounting for inflation, population growth, and a five percent buffer over six years. He attributed the majority of the overspending to the last three or four years, when rising property values increased tax receipts and budgets expanded accordingly. Ingoglia stated the county overspent by $443 million in the last fiscal year and urged voters to support property tax reform measures on the November ballot.

Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo made a surprise appearance to challenge Ingoglia's claims. Abruzzo noted that the Sheriff's Office comprises $1.1 billion of the county budget and fire rescue accounts for about $700 million, with the Board of County Commissioners controlling $609 million. He invited Ingoglia to review the budget details and stated the CFO has repeatedly ignored his public records requests for specifics on alleged overspending. Ingoglia responded that property tax increases reflect wasteful spending by "career politicians," not essential services or population needs.

cards.headline: Martin County man arrested on five animal cruelty counts after dead dog, starving animals found on Connors Highway property
cards.teaser: Jose Arreaga, 34, was arrested Tuesday after investigators found dogs in severe states of neglect, including one dead, at a tree farm on Southwest Connors Highway in Martin County.
cards.body:
Jose Arreaga, 34, identified as the manager of a property at 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on a warrant for five counts of animal cruelty, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. The investigation began June 2 when a community outreach manager contacted deputies after receiving an anonymous news tip with photographs allegedly showing deceased dogs on the property. On June 4, law enforcement responded to investigate.

Near the front of the residence, investigators found a loose cur mix female dog named Gorda, described as slightly underweight and severely infested with fleas. In a makeshift enclosure, they found the decomposed remains of a blonde, medium-sized dog with food and water bowls filled with sand and no evidence of recent use. Deputies also located a cream-colored male Anatolian shepherd collapsed beneath a tractor, so severely emaciated he initially appeared deceased. Both dogs were transported to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Three puppies were secured over the following day using a trap, all presenting with severe flea infestations and open sores. A brown domestic shorthair cat surrendered by Arreaga gave birth to four stillborn kittens the night of her arrival at the Humane Society. The charges are based on findings that all animals were deprived of adequate food, water, and nutritional care. Arreaga was held on $12,500 bond with conditions prohibiting him from owning or maintaining animals.

cards.teaser: Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.

Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records following his not guilty plea to driving under the influence after an arrest in March on Jupiter Island. The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County, announcing it will issue a subpoena on June 30 for records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization.

According to the filing, the subpoena will specifically seek any and all reports documenting statements Woods made regarding alcohol or chemical substance use, any and all drug screen results, and the name of the person who performed any testing. The filing was submitted by Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. Any objections to the subpoena must be delivered to the Assistant State Attorney within 10 days.

cards.headline: Delray Beach considers new e-bike rules after dangerous encounters on city streets
cards.teaser: City commissioner Juli Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding, and to require IDs and helmets for riders under 16.
cards.body:
Dangerous encounters with e-bikes and dirt bikes on Delray Beach streets have prompted city leaders to consider new rules. Fred Levy, from Highland Beach, who rides along A1A regularly, said unsafe riders make every trip unpredictable. "It's really scary for us bikers, really scary. I say every day I have like an incident where my sort of life passes in front of my eyes," Levy said. Frequent runner Kayla Genest has also noticed the problem, observing younger kids on e-bikes around the city doing wheelies and other tricks. City Commissioner Juli Casale said she has witnessed dangerous behavior firsthand, with riders moving in and out of traffic, sometimes going on the sidewalks.

Casale is pushing for a new ordinance to require helmets and identification for riders under 16, prevent speeding over 20 mph, and ban sidewalk riding. "The kids should not be riding over 20mph, they should be wearing helmets, they should carry identification and they should be very careful. I would be heartbroken if one of these kids got hurt in my city," Casale said. Resident Christopher Miles supports the new rules and hopes they prevent accidents. City staff will draft the ordinance and present it at a later meeting. Casale said the goal is to give officers the tools needed to enforce safety.

According to a statement from Tina Hatcher, the park is committed to providing a safe and family-friendly environment through a code of conduct, on-site police officers and a visible security presence.

While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. Guests can visit Rapids Water Park's website for additional details before planning their visit.

cards.teaser: West Palm Beach commissioners approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street, designed to divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from congested Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach commissioners approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, creating a direct connection between Fern Street and Clearwater Drive. The route is designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard, which drivers and city officials have identified as choke points in the downtown grid. City officials estimate the crossing would divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from the two congested corridors. Fern Street itself could be widened to five lanes to accommodate the expected increase in traffic volume.

The commission approved Resolution 119-26, a $3 million state-funded grant agreement through the Florida Department of Transportation, and Resolution 120-26F, covering associated funding appropriations. The total estimated cost for the roadway portion is $14.8 million. The remainder of the funding would come from existing city budget allocations and future sources including HUD grants, mobility fees, and CRA funding. The city is currently in the preliminary design phase. The project is expected to go out to bid as a design-build contract in fall 2026, with construction slated to begin in early 2027 and a target completion date of early 2028.

cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss ongoing and future efforts to revitalize the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss ongoing and future restoration efforts for the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians. Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County identified nutrient issues, vegetation problems, and management challenges affecting the lake. Meg Weinberger, who represents western Palm Beach County, also participated in the tour. Congressman and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds emphasized completing long-planned restoration projects, including a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels. Donalds also highlighted the need to address sediment buildup at the lake's bottom.

Friends of the Everglades acknowledged the value of the tour but argued the next governor should prioritize water storage and treatment projects south of Lake Okeechobee. Executive Director Eve Samples noted that Lake Okeechobee ranks among the most polluted lakes in North America and that the Southern Everglades are on track to fail phosphorus pollution limits with deadlines occurring this year. Samples stated that storage and treatment projects south of the lake would deliver greater value for taxpayer dollars than projects to the north, though she acknowledged northern storage could be part of a broader solution.

cards.headline: Jupiter weekend beach dance parties spark debate over sea turtle nesting disruption
cards.teaser: A popular weekend beach dance party at Jupiter beach access 55 is at the center of a debate over whether the gatherings are disrupting sea turtle nests during a record nesting season.
cards.body:
For the past three years, dozens and sometimes hundreds of people have gathered at beach access 55 in Jupiter for an event called "Happy Beach Dancing." The weekly meetup has drawn people of all ages, families, children, and dogs. Some residents are concerned the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests, though the movement is not to shut the event down but to ask the dancers to relocate during nesting season. Record numbers of loggerhead and leatherback sea turtle nests have been documented on Florida beaches this year.

Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at the nearby Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said Jupiter's beaches are among the densest nesting sites for loggerheads in the entire world, with 150 nests in this small area. She said just the fact that a large crowd gathered on the beach, no matter what they're doing, can deter the mama turtles from doing their nesting. The Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with the dance party organizers on Wednesday to discuss the issue. The founder of "Happy Beach Dancing" respectfully declined to comment on the controversy. The Town of Jupiter is gathering all interested stakeholders for this conversation.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents discuss housing concerns and community resources at library meetup
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents came to the Belle Glade Library to share their stories during a community meetup, covering topics from housing and affordability to local resources and upcoming events.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to share their stories and discuss pressing local issues. The conversation centered on housing affordability and available community resources. Local activist Delories Butts raised concerns about homelessness in the area, asking why the community cannot do more to help homeless people. Other residents shared positive perspectives about living in Belle Glade, with resident Veronica Bain expressing her love for the area.

Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, highlighted resources available to community members. The organization operates an ambassadorship program that selects three students from every school and mentors them throughout the year, holding them civically responsible for attending school board meetings and commission meetings. The meetup also addressed upcoming events, including a historic celebration. Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, which currently has eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. Let's Hear It events focus on uncovering the real stories that define communities.

cards.headline: Florida CFO claims Palm Beach County wasted $1.2 billion over last six years
cards.teaser: Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia held a news conference in Boca Raton Tuesday, claiming that Palm Beach County overspent by $1.23 billion since 2020 in excessive and wasteful spending.
cards.body:
Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia held a news conference Tuesday at Palm Beach State campus in Boca Raton, claiming that Palm Beach County tallied $1.23 billion since 2020 in "excessive and wasteful spending." Using his Florida Agency for Fiscal Oversight methodology, Ingoglia said this represented money collected that the county did not need to run local government, calculated as the amount over and above inflation, population growth and a five percent buffer over the last six years. He said the majority of that wasteful spending occurred over the last three or four years, coinciding with skyrocketing property values and tax receipts that caused budgets to expand. In the last fiscal year alone, Palm Beach County overspent by $443 million, according to Ingoglia.

Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo made a surprise appearance after the news conference and engaged in a two-minute back-and-forth with Ingoglia. Abruzzo countered that the majority of the county's budget goes to the sheriff's office at $1.1 billion and fire rescue at approximately $700 million, with the Board of County Commissioners operating on a $609 million budget. Abruzzo said Ingoglia has repeatedly ignored his public records requests for details on how the county is overspending, and urged the CFO to sit down for a working meeting to understand the budget. Ingoglia urged voters to support property tax reform on the November ballot.

hero.headline: Sargassum seaweed helps and hurts Florida sea turtles during nesting season
hero.body:
Sargassum seaweed presents a paradox for sea turtles along Florida's coastline. While many beachgoers view the brown seaweed as a nuisance that creates unpleasant odors and clutters shorelines, researchers at Florida Atlantic University explain that the situation is far more complex. The seaweed serves critical functions for sea turtles at different stages of their lives, even as excessive accumulation on beaches creates new hazards for hatchlings.

When sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests, they immediately swim toward the ocean. Once offshore, they seek out floating mats of sargassum that become their refuge during one of the most vulnerable periods of their lives. According to Emily Turla, laboratory coordinator at FAU's Marine Science Laboratory and a Ph.D. student, "Sargassum is an important habitat for young sea turtles when it's out offshore in the currents because that's where they swim out to right as they get off the beach." These floating mats provide essential shelter from predators, sources of food, and necessary habitat for young turtles navigating the open ocean.

Dr. Brian LaPointe, a research professor at FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, emphasizes the importance of sargassum in the broader marine ecosystem. "When sargassum is out in the open ocean, it is deemed essential fish habitat and it's also critical habitat for hatchlings leaving the beach," LaPointe said. The seaweed plays an important ecological role that extends beyond sea turtles alone.

The challenges emerge when excessive amounts of sargassum wash onto Florida's beaches. Large piles of seaweed create physical obstacles that hatchlings must navigate to reach the ocean. Turla notes that beachgoers sometimes observe hatchlings struggling within the seaweed accumulation. LaPointe explains that the extra time hatchlings spend maneuvering around these obstacles significantly extends their journey to the water, leaving them more vulnerable to predators during this critical period. As sea turtle nesting season progresses across South Florida, scientists stress that coastal communities must address an ongoing challenge: finding effective ways to manage excessive sargassum while preserving its essential ecological benefits. Understanding the dual nature of sargassum serves as an important reminder that even the most frustrating aspects of the natural environment can play vital roles in supporting local ecosystems and marine life.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties spark debate over sea turtle nests
cards.teaser: A weekly gathering called Happy Beach Dancing at Jupiter beach access 55 has drawn concerns from residents worried the events disrupt sea turtle nests during nesting season.
cards.body:
For the past three years, dozens and sometimes hundreds of people have gathered at Jupiter beach access 55 for an event called "Happy Beach Dancing." The weekly meetup has drawn people of all ages, families, children, and dogs. Some residents are concerned the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests, though the movement is not to shut the event down but to ask the dancers to relocate during nesting season.

Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at the Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said Jupiter's beaches are among the densest nesting sites for loggerheads in the entire world, with 150 nests in this small area. She said the fact that a large crowd gathered on the beach, no matter what they're doing, can deter mama turtles from nesting. The Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with the dance party organizers on Wednesday to discuss the issue. Isabel Nylen, a longtime Jupiter resident who has attended several dance events, said she understands both sides. The woman who founded "Happy Beach Dancing" respectfully declined to comment on the controversy. The Town of Jupiter is gathering all interested stakeholders for this conversation.

cards.headline: Florida prosecutors to subpoena Tiger Woods medical records in Jupiter Island DUI case
cards.teaser: The State of Florida will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.
cards.body:
The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County, announcing it will issue a subpoena on June 30 for records related to Tiger Woods' treatment or hospitalization. According to the filing, the subpoena will specifically seek any and all reports documenting statements Woods made regarding alcohol or chemical substance use, any and all drug screen results, and the name of the person who performed any testing.

The filing was submitted by Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. Any objections to the subpoena must be delivered to the Assistant State Attorney within 10 days. Woods pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following his arrest in March on Jupiter Island.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach ends youth supervision policy
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy that required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The park said the policy was intermittent and pulled in and out based on work with local authorities and social media trends. While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day.

In a statement, Tina Hatcher said the park is committed to providing a safe and family-friendly environment for guests at all times, working hand in hand with local officials and monitoring social media trends while upholding strict safety standards through a code of conduct, on-site police officers and a visible security presence. Guests can visit Rapids Water Park's website for additional details before planning their visit.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom sets up free food pantry outside home
cards.teaser: Jacquelyn Koester set up a Little Free Pantry outside her Hobe Sound home to help neighbors stretch their budgets as food costs rise.
cards.body:
Jacquelyn Koester set up a Little Free Pantry just steps from her home behind the Hobe Sound Public Library to help neighbors stretch their budgets amid rising food costs. The pantry is stocked with food and baby essentials for families struggling with higher prices. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," Koester said. What began as a simple Facebook post to ensure local families could access basic necessities has grown into a steady source of support available to anyone in need with no questions asked.

When gas and food prices increased, the pantry emptied faster than Koester could replace items. She put out a call for help on Facebook, and the community response has been overwhelming, with donations regularly filling the shelves. "Someone posted in the Facebook group anonymously saying I drove up from Jupiter for this, this is going to help get me through my week," Koester said. Those messages motivate her to maintain the pantry. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said.

hero.headline: Rapids Water Park hosts free admission for dads June 20-21, joins global water safety effort
hero.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach is offering free admission for fathers on June 20-21 during Father's Day weekend. The park, located at 6566 N. Military Trail, is also launching special events throughout the summer to appeal to different age groups. According to Greg Fuller, the park's general manager, families should take advantage of the free admission opportunity for dads this weekend.

The water park is bringing back Adults Night events designed for guests 21 and older. Elliott Russell, director of marketing and sales, explained that these nighttime events feature music, glow items, and exclusive access to the park's main attractions. Attendees can enjoy the slides, lazy river, and wave pool under the stars during these special adult-only sessions. The park is also introducing new food offerings this season, including specialty funnel cakes and other viral-style treats that will be available to guests.

On June 25, Rapids Water Park will participate in the World's Largest Swim Lesson, joining Live Like Jake and participants from around the world. This coordinated event aims to raise awareness about water safety and educate people of all ages on proper swimming techniques and safety practices. The park's involvement in this global initiative reflects a commitment to promoting water safety in the community beyond typical entertainment offerings.

Rapids Water Park operates daily with multiple ticket package options available for visitors planning their summer outings. Whether families are interested in the Father's Day weekend promotion, adults want to experience the glow-filled nighttime events, or guests of any age want to participate in the water safety lesson later in the month, the park is positioning itself as a hub for summer entertainment and education. For more information about the park's events, hours, and ticket options, visitors can contact the park directly or visit their official website.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library System summer reading challenge runs through July 31 with prizes
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, which runs through July 31 with free activities, incentives and grand prizes.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31, under the theme "Unearth a Story." Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

The challenge offers age-specific prizes. Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each branch is hosting special events including children's story times, craft sessions, adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances throughout the challenge. The program is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce displays live Florida coastal habitats
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium is inviting visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats with rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district.
cards.body:
Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. According to Hoffman, the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits, and he told WPTV the aquarium is "the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast." The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms, including a barracuda that measures just four inches. The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced by the live displays. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores house adoptable cats during Palm City shelter renovations
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City, with many cats temporarily shifted to store locations.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is temporarily housing adoptable cats at its two thrift stores while its Palm City shelter undergoes renovations. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, shifting many cats to the store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside unique items for sale at both thrift stores. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted. The organization welcomes donations of gently used goods and is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

hero.headline: Florida Chamber unveils 100 finalists for Coolest Thing Made in Florida competition
hero.body:
The Florida Chamber of Commerce and FloridaCommerce announced the 100 products competing in the second annual Coolest Thing Made in Florida competition. The bracket-style tournament is designed to celebrate products manufactured across the state while highlighting an industry that provides employment to more than 430,000 Floridians at an average annual wage of $86,405.

This year's competition reached a significant milestone by featuring manufacturers from all 67 Florida counties for the first time. "That achievement reflects the strength, diversity, and statewide impact of Florida's manufacturing sector," said Florida Chamber President and CEO Mark Wilson. "From rural communities to major metropolitan areas, manufacturers are creating jobs, driving innovation, and helping secure Florida's future as we work toward our Florida 2030 Blueprint goal of becoming a Top 5 state for manufacturing jobs." The competition received hundreds of nominations from manufacturers, employees and consumers throughout the state.

The 100 finalists represent the breadth of Florida's manufacturing capabilities, spanning aerospace and defense technologies, consumer goods, industrial equipment and agricultural products. Public voting is currently underway to narrow the field to the Top 32, with voting continuing through July 1. The remaining products will advance through a head-to-head tournament bracket leading to the selection of the 2026 Coolest Thing Made in Florida winner.

Florida Chamber and FloridaCommerce officials plan to visit the two finalist manufacturers during National Manufacturing Week in October before announcing the overall winner at the Florida Chamber's Future of Florida Forum and Annual Meeting later that month. The competition is intended to provide recognition for the state's premier homegrown products while underscoring manufacturing's significance to Florida's economy and workforce development.

cards.headline: Florida AFL-CIO endorses Amanda Green in Congressional District 2 race
cards.teaser: Democrat Amanda Green secured the backing of the Florida AFL-CIO for Florida's 2nd Congressional District, a seat now open and drawing a crowded field.
cards.body:
Democrat Amanda Green has secured the backing of the Florida AFL-CIO as she campaigns for Florida's 2nd Congressional District. The endorsement became official at the AFL-CIO's annual COPE Endorsing Convention in Orlando, following a recommendation from the Northwest Florida Federation of Labor. The organization stated that Green has a vision to build the strength of workers and family farmers and is committed to delivering on issues including lowering prices, access to food, higher wages, preserving and expanding social security, and universal, free-at-the-point-of-service healthcare. Green, who has already picked up endorsements from former U.S. Representative Allen Boyd and Leon County Sheriff Walt McNeil, called the AFL-CIO's support an honor.

Florida's 2nd Congressional District covers a broad swath of North Florida and the Panhandle. The seat is currently held by Republican U.S. Representative Neal Dunn, who is stepping aside after announcing he will not seek another term. The district leans heavily Republican, with more than 59 percent of voters in CD 2 supporting Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential race, while just 40 percent backed Democrat Kamala Harris. This year's contest has drawn a dozen candidates to the ballot, including several prominent Republicans.

cards.headline: Former Senate Agriculture Chair Denise Grimsley backs Ben Butler in Congressional District 9
cards.teaser: Former Senate Agriculture Chair Denise Grimsley is spearheading a wave of endorsements for Republican Ben Butler as he seeks to represent Florida's 9th Congressional District.
cards.body:
Former Senate Agriculture Chair Denise Grimsley is leading a slate of endorsements for Republican Ben Butler in Florida's 9th Congressional District. The endorsements also include former state Rep. Cary Pigman and former Florida Forestry Association President Jimmy Beilling. Grimsley, who served in the state Senate from 2012 to 2018 after eight years in the House, chaired the Senate Agriculture Committee during her tenure. She said Butler's experience as a dairy farmer and cattle rancher gives him firsthand knowledge of the issues facing Florida families and producers. Butler, a ninth-generation Floridian, sits on the South Florida Water Management District Governing Board and has made his rural roots and agricultural experience central to his campaign message.

Pigman described Butler as a practical problem-solver with a track record of community service, noting that good leaders listen, solve problems, and put people ahead of politics. Beilling argued that the district's farming communities need a representative who understands their challenges and will fight for their interests in Washington. Florida's 9th Congressional District includes all of Osceola County and portions of Orange and Polk counties. The seat is currently held by Democrat Darren Soto, who won re-election under the previous, more Democratic-leaning district lines. The new map has shifted the political landscape: more than 58% of voters in CD 9 backed Republican Donald Trump in 2024, making the district a top target for the GOP this cycle.

cards.headline: Panama City native Austin Rogers gains Bay County clerk and retired Air Force general backing in Congressional District 2
cards.teaser: Austin Rogers announced the backing of Bill Kinsaul, the Bay County Clerk of Court and Comptroller, and Darryl Roberson, a retired Air Force Lieutenant General.
cards.body:
Panama City native Austin Rogers announced endorsements from Bill Kinsaul, the longtime Bay County Clerk of Court and Comptroller, and Darryl Roberson, a retired Air Force Lieutenant General who commanded the 325th Fighter Wing at Tyndall Air Force Base and later led the Air Force's Air Education and Training Command. Kinsaul said Rogers is grounded in faith, guided by integrity, and committed to small-town values that make North Florida strong. He stated that Rogers understands families, churches, farms, small businesses, and local communities are the backbone of the district, and that Rogers will go to Washington to fight for conservative principles and defend constitutional freedoms.

Roberson, who led Tyndall during his tenure as wing commander, said he has known Rogers for over 30 years and described him as hardworking, intelligent, and polite. Roberson stated Rogers is exceptionally well qualified to serve the community and nation in Congress. Rogers graduated from Mosley High School and earned his law degree from Duke University before serving as chief counsel for Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans under Lindsey Graham and Chuck Grassley. The Republican Primary on Aug. 18 also features Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power, attorney and top fundraiser Keith Gross, and a roster of veterans and local officials competing in the solidly red Panhandle and Big Bend district.

cards.headline: Crowded Primary ballots in South Florida reflect structural constraints on Black political power
cards.teaser: The Primary Election ballot in North Miami-Dade and South Broward counties shows a wave of candidates following Frederica Wilson's announcement that she will not seek re-election.
cards.body:
Following Frederica Wilson's historic announcement that she will not seek re-election, a massive political cascade has been triggered in North Miami-Dade and South Broward counties. State Senators are running for Congress, state representatives are vying for the Senate, and a wave of new and familiar faces is stepping up to fill resulting vacancies on School Boards, County Commissions and municipal Councils. Fedrick Ingram, Secretary-Treasurer of the American Federation of Teachers, argues that what is being witnessed in the 24th Congressional District is not unchecked personal ambition but the predictable consequence of a voting map designed to constrict Black electoral opportunity.

Ingram contends that for over a decade, gerrymandering by the Florida Legislature has systematically packed Black voters into a limited number of districts while diluting their influence everywhere else. When Wilson, who has held the seat for nearly three decades across the School Board, Tallahassee and Washington, decides to pass the torch, the dam breaks. The sheer volume of candidates reflects a massive, pent-up reservoir of talent and energy and a profound desire to serve a community that is too often left behind. Ingram calls on candidates who do not prevail in August to immediately fold their operations, volunteers and voter lists into the coordinated Democratic ticket for November to avoid fracturing communities during the General Election.

cards.headline: Knicks-Spurs NBA Finals draws most viewers in 28 years
cards.teaser: The Knicks-Spurs NBA Finals averaged 20.6 million viewers per game on ABC and ESPN, marking the most-watched Finals in 28 years.
cards.body: The Knicks-Spurs NBA Finals was the most-watched NBA Finals in 28 years, averaging 20.6 million viewers per game on ABC and ESPN. The Knicks series-clinching win in Game 5 averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked with 33 million viewers, marking the most-watched Game 5 in 28 years. The league also had its most-watched postseason in 28 years across ABC/ESPN, Amazon Prime Video and NBC/Peacock, according to the NBA.

cards.teaser: The 2026 Florida Python Challenge is scheduled to begin 23 days from Wednesday, June 17, 2026.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie residents to receive credits after $24 million settlement with former trash hauler
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents will get money back after the city received a $24 million settlement with their former trash hauler, Waste Pro. The city voted to return all of it to residents through property tax credits.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive credits on their property tax bills following a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro, the city's former trash hauler. The city council voted unanimously to distribute all settlement funds back to residents who experienced service problems during 2021 and 2022. Rather than receiving checks, residents will see credits applied directly to their property tax bills. Mayor Shannon Martin stated, "From the beginning, I have maintained that the funds should be to benefit the residents who experienced the issues in 2021 and 2022."

The dispute between the city and Waste Pro began in 2021 when both parties filed lawsuits against each other. The city claimed the company breached its service contract and failed to meet required standards, while Waste Pro attributed the problems to pandemic-related labor shortages. The settlement allows the city to recover costs from the litigation, a new waste site, and the transition to a new service provider. Not all residents will receive equal credits, as the city tailored payouts based on the extent of service disruptions experienced by different property owners.

More than 5,700 properties with the same owner continuously since 2022 will receive $364 credits. The city determined these households experienced the most significant problems, including service interruptions, during Waste Pro's breach of contract. Councilman David Pickett explained the reasoning, saying, "They're the ones that suffered who went through the litigation, and now it's time to reward them for the suffering they did." Thousands of other homes will receive $64 credits due to rate increases that occurred during the service breach period.

Additional categories of properties will also receive $64 credits. The city identified 24,676 properties where ownership changed since 2022 but cannot determine whether the changes resulted from trusts, marriages, divorces, or relocations. Former owners cannot be reached to verify circumstances. The same $64 credit applies to 13,241 newly constructed properties, as these households also paid rate increases. However, residents who sold one home and purchased another within the city during this period may submit documentation proving continuous ownership and claim the remaining $300 credit on the following year's tax bill. The city will establish the claims process after review by city staff and the legal department, with a 180-day window for submissions. One resident, Kelly Lee, expressed satisfaction with the council's approach, saying, "I was pleasantly surprised with the outcome. The city presented well thought out plans."

cards.headline: Republican lawmakers tour Lake Okeechobee, discuss water quality and restoration efforts
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday, discussing ongoing and future efforts to revitalize the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss restoration efforts for the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians. Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County and Meg Weinberger, who represents western Palm Beach County, joined the tour alongside conservation groups for a firsthand look at the lake's challenges and progress. Overdorf said the area faces nutrient issues, vegetation issues, and management problems that converge in one particular location.

Congressman and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds participated in the tour and emphasized completing long-planned restoration projects. He highlighted a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels. Friends of the Everglades Executive Director Eve Samples acknowledged the value of leaders seeing the lake firsthand but argued the next governor should prioritize water storage and treatment projects south of Lake Okeechobee instead. Samples noted the lake is one of the most polluted lakes in North America and cited urgent phosphorus pollution deadlines facing the Southern Everglades this year. She said storing and treating water south of the lake would provide the greatest return for taxpayer dollars and allow water to reach the Southern Everglades, which needs more fresh clean water.

cards.headline: Martin County residents push for public pool at high school, call for November referendum
cards.teaser: Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an.
cards.body:
Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an affordable resource for swim education. Patty Beonde, whose brother drowned at 30 years old, spoke at the meeting. She said her brother was caught in an undertow and had never had swimming lessons. Ricki Stein, a Martin County resident, said free access is key to getting children comfortable in the water. Dick Landrum, another Martin County resident, said affordability is central to the effort, noting that several venues in Martin County teach people how to swim but most are costly.

The nonprofit Martin Swims asked local leaders to put a referendum on the November ballot that would create a fund to establish community pools. They suggested residents pay less than $10 a year per property to fund the pool on the Martin County High School campus. Both county and school district leaders expressed support for the idea. Martin County Commissioner Ed Ciampi said he is in favor of letting the public decide on the importance of swimming education. Martin County School District Superintendent Michael Maine said he is already making plans to set up a meeting with Martin Swims to explore the logistics. Dr. Blanche Wells, president of Martin Swims, said the cause is personal and urgent and that those involved are devoted to it because it is life-saving.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach approves nearly $15 million Fern Street railroad crossing project
cards.teaser: West Palm Beach commissioners have approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street to reduce congestion on Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach commissioners have approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street designed to reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads. The project would construct a new at-grade railroad crossing between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, creating a direct connection between Fern Street and Clearwater Drive. The route is designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard, which drivers and city officials have identified as choke points in the downtown grid. Fern Street itself could be widened to five lanes to accommodate expected traffic volume increases. City officials estimate the crossing would divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from the two congested corridors.

The commission approved two resolutions at its meeting: Resolution 119-26, a $3 million state-funded grant agreement through the Florida Department of Transportation, and Resolution 120-26F, covering associated funding appropriations. The total estimated cost for the roadway portion is $14.8 million, with the remainder coming from existing city budget allocations and future sources including HUD grants, mobility fees, and CRA funding. The city is currently in the preliminary design phase. The project is expected to go out to bid as a design-build contract in fall 2026, with construction slated to begin in early 2027 and a target completion date of early 2028.

cards.headline: Delray Beach considers new e-bike rules after dangerous encounters on city streets
cards.teaser: Dangerous encounters with e-bikes and dirt bikes on Delray Beach streets have city leaders considering new rules, with residents and officials speaking out about stricter regulations.
cards.body:
City Commissioner Juli Casale has witnessed dangerous e-bike behavior firsthand, including riders moving in and out of traffic, sometimes riding on sidewalks while wearing masks. She is pushing for a new ordinance to crack down on speeding and sidewalk riding, and to require helmets and identification for riders under 16. Casale said kids should not ride over 20 mph, should wear helmets, should carry identification, and should be very careful, adding she would be heartbroken if one of these kids got hurt in the city.

Fred Levy, from Highland Beach, who rides along A1A regularly, described the risks of the scenic route. He said it's really scary for bikers and that he has an incident nearly every day where his life passes in front of his eyes. Frequent runner Kayla Genest said she has seen a lot of younger kids on e-bikes around the city doing wheelies and other kinds of tricks that are dangerous. City staff will draft the ordinance and present it at a later meeting. cards.headline: Sargassum helps and hurts Florida's sea turtles during nesting season
cards.teaser: Researchers say sargassum provides important habitat for young sea turtles offshore, but excessive amounts washing ashore can create obstacles for hatchlings trying to reach the ocean.
cards.body:
Emily Turla, laboratory coordinator at Florida Atlantic University's Marine Science Laboratory and a Ph.D. student, explained that sargassum serves as critical habitat for young sea turtles when it floats offshore in ocean currents. After hatching, sea turtles swim away from shore during their first vulnerable days, and floating mats of sargassum provide shelter from predators, food sources, and essential habitat during this critical stage of their lives.

Dr. Brian LaPointe, research professor with FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, noted that sargassum plays an important role in the marine ecosystem as essential fish habitat and critical habitat for hatchlings leaving the beach. However, problems arise when excessive amounts of sargassum wash ashore. Large piles of seaweed become obstacles for hatchlings attempting to reach the ocean, and the extra time spent navigating around the seaweed increases their vulnerability to predators. As sea turtle nesting season continues across South Florida, researchers say finding ways to manage excessive sargassum while preserving its ecological benefits remains an important challenge for coastal communities and a reminder that even frustrating aspects of the natural environment play crucial roles in the local ecosystem.

hero.headline: Florida Prosecutors to Subpoena Tiger Woods Medical Records After March DUI Arrest on Jupiter Island

The legal process includes a set timeline for response. Anyone wishing to object to the subpoena must submit those objections to the Assistant State Attorney within ten days of the June 15 filing date. This notice and objection period allows Woods' legal team or medical providers to challenge the request if they believe it violates privacy rights or other legal protections before the records must be surrendered.

Woods was arrested in March on Jupiter Island after authorities responded to a traffic crash. He subsequently entered a not guilty plea to the DUI charge, setting the stage for the current discovery process. The subpoena for medical records represents standard procedure as prosecutors build their case, seeking documentation that could be relevant to establishing the circumstances surrounding the arrest and any potential impairment.

cards.headline: Republican Lawmakers Tour Lake Okeechobee to Discuss Water Quality and Restoration
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday, viewing restoration efforts for a waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss efforts to revitalize one of Florida's most important waterways. The lake provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians and has been called the liquid heart of the Everglades. The tour included Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County, Rep. Meg Weinberger of western Palm Beach County, and Congressman Byron Donalds. Overdorf said the area faces nutrient issues, vegetation issues, and management issues that are interconnected. Donalds said the focus should be on completing long-planned restoration projects, including a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels and address sediment in the lake bottom.

Friends of the Everglades acknowledged the value of the tour but argued for a different approach. Executive Director Eve Samples said Lake Okeechobee is one of the most polluted lakes in North America, and the Southern Everglades are on track to fail phosphorus pollution limits with deadlines kicking in this year. Samples argued that the greatest return for taxpayer dollars would come from storage and treatment projects south of Lake Okeechobee rather than north of the lake, which could send clean water to the Southern Everglades.
